newsitem.title: USA: Police say author Dorris a suicide.
newsitem.headline: Police say author Dorris a suicide.

text.p: Author Michael Dorris, whose bestselling book about raising a brain-damaged child, "The Broken Cord," brought attention to the problem of foetal alcohol syndrome, committed suicide after checking into a motel here, police said on Monday.

Concord police said Dorris, 52, an author, anthropolgist and founder of Dartmouth College's Native American Studies Programme, suffocated himself on Friday with a plastic bag after checking into the Brick Tower Motel under an assumed name.
Police said a note was left at the scene but they declined to disclose its details. An autopsy report from the state medical examiner was expected on Tuesday.

Dorris, who was married to bestselling novelist Louise Erdrich, co-wrote "The Crown of Columbus" with her in 1991 after a publisher agreed to pay the couple $1.5 million on the basis of a five-page outline.

Born of mixed Irish, French and American Indian ancestry, Dorris was the author of two novels, including the recently published "Cloud Chamber," but was best known for "The Broken Cord," his bestselling 1989 memoir of adopting an American Indian child who suffered from foetal alcohol syndrome.

Dorris, who was the first unmarried American male to legally adopt a child, told the story of his son Abel, who suffered brain damage as a result of his mother's heavy drinking. The youth died at 23 in a car accident in 1992.

In an article for the Minneapolis Star Tribune last year, Dorris wrote, "He lived for 23 years, endured daily loneliness and confusion and hardship and frustration, and in all that time he never once did anything that was intentionally cruel or hurtful to another living creature.
"He was maddening in his inabilty to learn from experience, to grasp a larger picture. ... If only he had been able to learn how to cross the street in accordance with a green light."
The book drew international attention to the dangers children face if their mothers drink during pregnancy and it led to moves in Congress to issue warnings about the risks.
Esquire Magazine reported in March that Dorris and Erdrich, who were married in 1981, were in the process of divorcing. He had been teaching in Minneapolis this year while on leave from Dartmouth.
Dorris' friends were shocked at the news of his death.

"Mike was ... a great friend and a superb teacher. He is responsible for creation of the Native American programme at Dartmouth. Because he was the most determined of workers, that programme was and is a success," said Peter Burling, a friend.

Dartmouth College President James Freedman called Dorris "a rare and devoted friend. The Native American Studies Programme will stand as an enduring contribution to Dartmouth and to American higher education."
